source_text: Consequitur et Zacchei domus salutem. quo merito? numquid uel ille crediderat Christum a (deo) Marcionis uenisse? atquin adhuc in auribus erat omnium uox illa caeci: miserere mei, Iesu, fili Dauid, et: omnis populus laudes referebant deo, non Marcionis, sed Dauid. enimuero Zaccheus, etsi allophylus, fortasse tamen aliqua notitia scripturarum ex commercio Iudaico adflatus, — plus est autem, (si) et ignorans Esaiam — praecepta eius impleuerat: confringito, inquit, panem tuum esurienti et non habentes tectum in domum tuam inducito — hoc cum maxime agebat, exceptum domo sua pascens dominum — et nudum si uideris, contegito; hoc cum maxime promittebat, in omnia misericordiae opera dimidium substantiae offerens, dissoluens uiolentiorum contractuum obnexus et dimittens conflictatos in laxamentum et omnem conscriptionem iniquam dissipans dicendo: et si cui quid per calumniam eripui, quadruplum reddo. itaque dominus: hodie, inquit, salus huic domui. testimonium dixit salutaria esse quae praeceperat prophetes creatoris. cum uero dicit: uenit enim filius hominis saluum facere quod periit, iam non contendo eum uenisse, ut saluum faceret quod perierat cuius fuerat et cui perierat quod saluum uenerat facere, sed in alterius quaestionis gradum dirigo. de homine agi nulla dubitatio est. hic cum ex duabus substantiis constet, ex corpore et anima, quaerendum est, ex qua substantiae specie perisse uideatur. si ex corpore, ergo corpus perierat, anima non. quod perierat saluum facit filius hominis: habet igitur et caro salutem, si ex anima perierat, animae perditio saluti destinatur: caro, quae non periit, salua est. si totus homo perierat ex utraque substantia, totus homo saluus fiat necesse est, et elisa est sententia haereticorum negantium carnis salutem. iam et Christus creatoris confirmatur, qui secundum creatorem totius hominis salutem pollicebatur. Seruorum quoque parabola, qui secundum rationem feneratae pecuniae dominicae diiudicantur, iudicem ostendit deum (tuum) etiam ex parte seueritatis, non tantum onerantem uerum et auferentem quod quis uideatur habuisse. aut si et haec creatorem finxerit, (austerum, tollentem quod non posuerit et metentem quod non seuerit,' hic quoque me ille instruit, cuius pecuniam ut fenerem edocet.
pass_a_gloss: It follows also the salvation of Zacchaeus' house. By what merit? Had he even believed that Christ came from the God of Marcion? But still in the ears of all was that voice of the blind man: have mercy on me, Jesus, Son of David, and: all the people were giving praise to God, not of Marcion, but of David. Indeed, Zacchaeus, although a foreigner, perhaps nonetheless had some knowledge of the scriptures from Jewish commerce, — it is more, however, if even ignoring Isaiah — had fulfilled his precepts: break, he says, your bread for the hungry and bring into your house those who have no shelter — this he was doing especially, having received the Lord into his house and feeding him — and if you see someone naked, clothe him; this he was promising especially, offering half of his substance for all works of mercy, dissolving the bonds of violent contracts and releasing those who were oppressed and dissipating every unjust conscription, saying: and if I have taken anything from someone by calumny, I will repay fourfold. And so the Lord says: today, salvation to this house. He gave testimony that the things which the prophet of the Creator had commanded were salutary. When, indeed, he says: for the Son of Man came to save what was lost, I no longer argue that he came to save what was lost, whose it was and to whom what was lost, for which he came to save, but I direct to the level of another question. There is no doubt that it is a matter of a human being. Since this human being consists of two substances, body and soul, it must be asked, from which substance's kind it seems to have perished. If from the body, then the body had perished, not the soul. The Son of Man saves what had perished: therefore, the flesh also has salvation, if it perished from the soul, the loss of the soul is destined for salvation: the flesh, which did not perish, is saved. If the whole human being had perished from both substances, it is necessary that the whole human being be saved, and the sentence of the heretics who deny the salvation of the flesh is destroyed. Now also the Christ of the Creator is confirmed, who promised the salvation of the whole human being according to the Creator. Also the parable of the servants, who are judged according to the reason of the lent money of the Lord, shows God as judge, even in the part of severity, not only burdening but also taking away what someone seems to have had. Or if he also feigned this as the Creator, (being austere, taking away what he did not put and reaping what he did not sow), this also instructs me, whose money he teaches as a loan.

choices.why: to specify the God of Marcion

bible_refs.note: the Son of Man came to save what was lost

pass_b_english: Salvation comes to Zacchaeus' house as well. On what grounds? Had he perhaps believed that Christ came from Marcion's god? But the blind man's cry still rang in everyone's ears: 'Have mercy on me, Jesus, Son of David,' and the whole crowd was giving praise to God — not Marcion's god, but David's. (Luke 19:9-10) Zacchaeus, for all his foreign blood, may have picked up some scriptural knowledge through Jewish trade connections — more impressively, he fulfilled the prophet's commands even if he never read Isaiah: 'Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house' — which he did above all by welcoming the Lord into his home and feeding him — 'and when you see the naked, clothe them' — which he pledged above all by offering half his estate for every work of mercy, tearing up the bonds of predatory contracts, releasing the oppressed, canceling every unjust levy, and declaring, 'If I have extorted anything from anyone, I repay it fourfold.' (Luke 19:9-10) So the Lord says: 'Today salvation has come to this house.' He testified that the Creator's prophet had commanded what brings salvation. (Luke 19:9-10)

When he adds, 'For the Son of Man came to save what was lost,' I no longer waste time arguing that he came to save what was lost, whose it was, and to whom it was lost, since he came to save it. (Luke 19:10; Matthew 18:11) I move the debate to the next level. No one doubts we are talking about a human being. Since a human being consists of two substances — body and soul — the question is: from which substance did the loss occur? If from the body, then the body perished, not the soul. The Son of Man saves what perished: therefore the flesh has salvation too. If the loss came from the soul, the soul's loss is destined for salvation; the flesh, which did not perish, is already safe. If the whole human being perished from both substances, then the whole human being must be saved — and the heretics' verdict denying the flesh's salvation collapses. Now the Christ of the Creator stands confirmed, the one who promised the salvation of the whole human being according to the Creator. (Luke 19:10; Matthew 18:11)

The parable of the servants, judged according to the accounting of the Lord's entrusted money, shows God as judge even on the side of severity — not only demanding a return but taking away what someone merely seemed to have. (Luke 19:9-10) Or if the Creator fabricated this severity too — 'a harsh man, taking what he did not deposit and reaping what he did not sow' — that very line instructs me, since it is his money he teaches me to invest. (Luke 19:9-10)

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological argument regarding the two substances (body and soul) and the salvation of the flesh. Pass A preserves the Latin syntax and nuances, while Pass B provides a fluent English rendering with appropriate scripture citations (Luke 19:9-10, Matthew 18:11) that match the content. The distinction between 'the God of Marcion' and 'the Creator' is maintained.
